name: Shape-up / line-up

card.summary: A shape-up (line-up, edge-up) is a barber's sharp outline of the hairline, temples, sideburns and neckline with clippers or a trimmer, giving a crisp frame around the face.
card.aka: edge up, line up, shape up
card.note: Edges grow back within days to weeks, so the look needs regular touch-ups.

quick.overview:
A shape-up, also called a line-up or edge-up, is a grooming step in which a barber uses clippers or a trimmer to cut clean, straight edges along the front hairline, temples, sideburns and the neckline. It is common in barbershops and often goes with a fade or short cut.
The visible result is a defined hairline and a clearly outlined haircut. Barbers and customers describe it as making the hair look intentional and the forehead and face shape appear framed.
quick.how: A barber outlines the hairline, often with a guard-less trimmer or edger, and squares or rounds the corners depending on preference. It is usually done with a haircut and refreshed every one to two weeks by people who like the sharpest edges. A fade tapers the sides, while the line-up defines the outline.
quick.risks: The main risks are razor bumps or irritation along the edges, and an edge cut too far back can move the hairline. People with a receding hairline sometimes discuss how a line-up changes its look.

lead: The shape-up, line-up or edge-up is the practice of cleaning and sharpening the outline of a haircut: the front hairline, temples, sideburns and the back of the neck. Barbers use trimmers or outliner clippers to cut crisp lines [1][2].

Its appearance effect is to frame the face. A sharp hairline gives the cut definition, can make the hairline look even and cleaner, and pairs with short fades and tapers, in which a fine blade blends the sides into the top [2]. Wikipedia notes that sideburn length and neck-edge height change how the face looks, for example that a shorter neck or chin suits a somewhat higher neck edge [2].

Grokipedia places the shape-up's origins in African American barbering traditions of the 1980s, alongside the rise of hip-hop culture, and links it with a groomed, structured look in urban communities; that page names no inventor and its hairstyle claims rest on barbershop websites [1]. Wikipedia's article on fades describes the closest related concept, edging, as outlining the lower hairline around the sideburns, ears and nape with outliner or edger clippers [2].

angle.text: The line-up changes how clean and defined the outline of a haircut looks, and the result lasts until the edges grow back.

infobox: Every one to two weeks for the sharpest edges [1]

paras: In a fade, a coarse clipper blade is used on the sides and back and a fine blade at the sideburns, with the lines blended for a smooth transition [2]. The line-up is the finishing outline on top of that work, drawn around the edges of the hair. The result is straight, angular lines that follow or sharpen the head's natural contour [1].

Wikipedia's description of edging distinguishes a two-line cut, in which the hair is outlined around the ears and down the neck and the nape is tapered to the skin with a fine blade, from a one-line or block cut, in which the nape outline is shaved so hair meets skin abruptly. Block napes can be squared or rounded, with squared or rounded corners [2]. Outliner or edger clippers have a very fine blade and no taper lever, and are used for the defined arch around the ears and for block napes [2].

Short back-and-sides cuts, the base on which fades and edging sit, trace to the Roman legionary haircut, returned in the Renaissance and the Regency era, and became the norm for professional men by about 1910; the undercut was adopted by hipster subculture in the 2010s [2]. Grokipedia dates the shape-up as a distinct style to 1980s African American barbering [1].

The tools have their own history. Wikipedia credits Serbian barber Nikola Bizumic with manual clippers around 1855, and Leo J. Wahl with the first patented electric hair clipper in 1921; Andis and Oster entered the electric market in the same period, Oster in 1928 [3]. The first barber school is reported as opened in Chicago in 1893 by A. B. Moler [4].

Barbers use clippers, trimmers and outliner or edger clippers for the lines [2]. Blade numbering matters for what the skin looks like afterward: Oster's fine (zero) blades leave very short stubble, equivalent to about five hours to under two days of growth [3]. Clippers use magnetic, rotary or pivot motors, and manufacturers advise lubricating blades with oil or aerosol clipper spray [3].

Many US states require a barber licence, with training of roughly 800 to 2,000 hours depending on the state, and in some states, such as Maryland and Pennsylvania, only licensed barbers may use straight razors [4].

Wikipedia describes Black-owned barbershops in the United States as influential businesses since around the turn of the 19th century, and quotes scholar Trudier Harris calling the Black barbershop a gathering place and retreat from daily pressures [4]. Researchers have used barbershops as venues for health education; a cluster randomised trial in 24 pairs of Philadelphia barbershops delivered barber-led HIV and STI risk-reduction content to young African American men [4][7]. The line-up is a routine part of this setting, usually refreshed on a regular schedule by repeat customers.

Male-pattern hair loss usually begins with a receding front hairline above the temples and at the crown, and by age 50 about half of men are affected according to a source cited by Wikipedia [6]. Barbers and customers discuss how the position of the line-up interacts with a recession; Grokipedia notes that the style needs skilled execution to avoid unnatural angles [1]. On looksmax.org, users post photos asking whether to trim, even out or reshape their hair, with replies commenting on how a cut suits their face [8].

Grokipedia says improper tooling can cause unnatural angles or skin irritation [1]. Very close shaving of the edges can lead to pseudofolliculitis barbae (razor bumps), in which shaved hair curls back into the skin and causes inflammation; Wikipedia reports it mostly affects people with curly or coarse hair, that a related condition occurs on the back of the neck, and that a keratin gene polymorphism is linked to it [5].

For people prone to it, Wikipedia says studies suggest leaving hair about 0.5 to 1 mm long, for example with a trimmer on its lowest setting, and that letting hair grow for three to four weeks lets most lesions subside [5]. Untreated, it can cause keloid scarring [5].

timeline.event: Nikola Bizumic is credited with manual hair clippers.[3]
A. B. Moler founds a barber school in Chicago.[4]
Leo J. Wahl patents the first electric hair clipper.[3]
John Oster Manufacturing enters the electric clipper market.[3]
Grokipedia dates the shape-up as a distinct style to African American barbering of this decade.[1]
The undercut is adopted by hipster subculture while short back-and-sides stays popular with professionals.[2]
